title: Enterprise guarantee narrative and objection library
content:
Purpose:
This is a working playbook for field-facing teams (sales engineering, solutions, AE, and legal enablement) to frame Redwood’s dedicated/reserved inference offering to enterprise buyers who require predictable throughput, isolation, and contractual guarantees.

Audience & use cases:
- Procurement and vendor evaluation committees assessing SLA-backed inference capacity for customer-facing product features.
- Platform/Infra architects validating isolation guarantees between tenants and noisy neighbors.
- Finance teams modeling committed spend vs optional burst usage.
- Legal teams reviewing SLA language and remedies.

Core positioning pillars (short bullets for pitch decks & emails):
- Predictable throughput you can contract: reserved capacity mapped to token throughput and concurrent request targets, with canary-friendly rollouts and capacity guarantees.
- Strong isolation boundaries: dedicated GPU pools, per-customer KV-cache segregation, and network-level tenancy options (VPC/private deployments) for compliance-sensitive workloads.
- Measurable latency and availability commitments: SLOs tailored to customer profile (p95/p99 latency bands, availability tiers) with clear credits/escrow for violations.
- Operational transparency: token-level cost & latency traces, per-route dashboards, and audit logs to reconcile performance to invoices.
- Risk-reduction playbook: fallbacks to verified model variants, cross-region routing, and automatic throttling policies to preserve critical flows.

Buyer personas & quick scripts:
- Platform Architect (tech-first): emphasize isolation, KV caching per-tenant, predictable tail latency, ability to pin model versions, and observability hooks (traces, metrics, sampling).
  Script: "We deliver capacity that maps to effective throughput under your real workload distribution — not just idealized tokens. You can pin models and we surface traces per route so you can validate behavior before cutover."
- Procurement Lead (commercial): lead with commitment/discount structure and remedies.
  Script: "We offer tiered reserved commitments with built-in burst credits, objective SLOs, and credits that apply automatically on missed targets — so your procurement paperwork can specify measurable outcomes."
- Finance/FP&A: focus on unit economics, price predictability, and optimization levers.
  Script: "Committed capacity lowers per-token unit costs and we provide optimize reports (batching/quantization recommendations) to reduce long-term spend by X–Y%."

SLA framing (recommended defaults & negotiation ranges):
- Availability: 99.9% monthly for production reserved pools (negotiable to 99.95% for large customers). Remedy: service credits tier (5% invoice credit for first tier breach, escalating).
- Latency: p95 <= 300ms for short-text models (configurable based on model family & sequence length), p99 targets and credits only when p99 breaches more than X% of requests over a day.
- Throughput guarantee: ability to sustain N tokens/sec for committed SKU with a 10% burst buffer for short windows.
- Isolation guarantee: explicit language that committed pools will not be shared with third parties and noisy-tenant mitigation policies are enforced.
- Incident response & escalation: 24/7 platform & se-assigned on-call, defined RTO/RPO for control-plane outages, weekly postmortem within 7 business days for severity-1 incidents.

Sample contract clause (field copy — shorten before legal):
"Redwood shall allocate dedicated inference capacity sufficient to sustain the Customer's committed throughput (X tokens/sec) measured as average sustained throughput over 15-minute intervals. Should Redwood fail to meet the agreed throughput or availability SLOs, Customer will receive service credits equal to a percentage of the monthly committed fee, per the breach ladder specified in Schedule A."

Negotiation playbook (what to ask for / what to concede):
- Opening asks: baseline availability (99.9), clear throughput numbers, uninterrupted isolation statement, audit access for performance traces, 30-day notice for planned maintenance windows.
- Concessions we can make quickly: extended maintenance windows for lower SLAs, limited visibility into internal kernel-level metrics (share summarized traces instead), limited pilot discounts.
- Concessions that require legal/exec sign-off: higher availability (99.95+), revenue-backed indemnity items, extended financial remedies beyond credits.

Commercial packaging & price triggers (examples to use in proposals):
- Starter reserved band: small commitment (3–6 months), low discount, includes burst credits for spikes, suitable for evaluating production viability.
- Production reserved band: 12-month committed capacity with quantifiable throughput mapping and deeper discounts — includes SAT (service acceptance test) during onboarding and SRE-run playbook transfer.
- Enterprise reserved band: multi-year commitment, SLO customization, on-prem/VPC options, white-glove SRE support and priority routing.

Responding to common objections (script snippets):
- "We don’t want to pay for idle GPUs." -> "We layer burst credits, autoscaling and right-sized SKU recommendations (quantization + batching) that reduce average effective cost; reserved capacity also guarantees lower unit cost under predictable load — finance teams model break-evens in 6–9 months for customer-facing features."
- "How is this better than using managed endpoints from cloud vendors?" -> "Our runtime is optimized for inference throughput and cost (attention optimizations, KV caching, continuous batching). We provide predictable economics and enterprise-friendly SLAs and observability that cloud vendor endpoints generally don’t package together in a single committed offering."
- "What happens during outages?" -> "We provide cross-region fallback, automatic model-variant downgrade policies, and a documented incident playbook; high-severity incidents trigger customer-specific war-rooms and postmortems with action items."

Competitive notes (quick takeaways for AE & SE):
- Competitor A (vendor-managed endpoints): cheaper for ad-hoc, but lacks guaranteed isolation & deterministic throughput; weak observability.
- Competitor B (self-hosted inference runtimes): more control but higher ops cost and longer time-to-value; patchy enterprise-grade support and no single vendor SLA.
- Competitor C (single-cloud ML platform): good integration with cloud services but inconsistent latency under multi-tenant pressure and limited model-variant fallbacks.

Scoring matrix (for quick internal reference) — top three decision axes buyers care about:
- Throughput predictability: Redwood (+++) vs A (+) vs B (++) vs C (+)
- Isolation & compliance: Redwood (+++) vs A (+) vs B (++) vs C (+)
- Operational overhead: Redwood (+) vs A (++) vs B (-) vs C (+)
- Cost predictability: Redwood (+++) vs A (+) vs B (-) vs C (+)

Field-ready collateral to attach to proposals:
- Mapping table: committed SKU -> tokens/sec mapping for common models (guesstimates with caveats).
- Onboarding checklist: SAT steps, test load scripts, acceptance criteria.
- Appendix: sample SLA schedule, escalation contact template, and runbooks.

Open questions / TODOs (work-in-progress):
- Need precise certified throughput numbers per SKU for the most common open models (action: apply-load-tests from infra/benchmarks; owner: Evan; ticket: GTM-1287).
- Legal: draft tighter credit ladder for multi-year deals (owner: Maya).
- Finance: build a pricing worksheet that shows effective $/1K tokens for 3/12/36 month commitments (owner: Samir).

References & links:
- Slack thread #gtm-dedicated (internal objections + win stories)
- Confluence: PRO-3421 (SLA baseline language drafts)
- JIRA: GTM-1287 (throughput certification tests)

Notes to field (rough):
- Use the phrase "SLO-backed reserved throughput" in revenues decks (legal prefers "SLA" in contracts).
- For pilots, prefer short reserved windows with measurable acceptance criteria rather than pure on-demand trials (better to collect real traffic shape).
